subject: Banking
title: Continental Illinois: Too Big to Fail
description: One-minute skill: Continental Illinois: Too Big to Fail.

hook.text: In 1984, Continental Illinois was America's seventh-largest bank. It failed in what regulators called 'too big to fail.'

buildup.text: The bank had bought $1 billion in risky oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank.

discovery.text: Electronic bank runs arrived. Continental lost $10 billion in deposits via wire transfers in days, not weeks.

twist.text: The FDIC rescued every depositor, even those above the $100,000 insurance limit.

climax.text: Continental Illinois created the moral hazard problem: big banks get rescued, small banks don't.

punchline.text: Too big to fail. The phrase and the problem were born with Continental Illinois.

quiz.question: What term was coined during the Continental Illinois failure?

details.summary: Continental Illinois became the first bank officially deemed too big to fail in 1984 when the FDIC bailed out all depositors and creditors, including those above the insurance limit, to prevent a panic that could spread to other banks.
details.whyItMatters: Continental Illinois established the too-big-to-fail doctrine that still shapes banking today. The decision to protect all creditors created moral hazard that contributed to every subsequent banking crisis.
takeaways: Continental Illinois was the seventh-largest US bank when it failed
The FDIC protected all depositors and creditors, even those above insurance limits
The phrase too big to fail was coined during Congressional hearings on the bailout

faq.question: Why was Continental Illinois considered too big to fail?
faq.answer: Regulators found that 179 smaller banks had deposits at Continental exceeding their insurance limits. Allowing it to fail would have triggered cascading failures at these banks, potentially causing a nationwide banking panic.

faq.question: How did the Continental Illinois bailout create moral hazard?
faq.answer: By protecting all creditors, the government signaled that large bank depositors and bondholders had implicit government backing. This reduced the incentive for creditors to monitor bank risk-taking, encouraging more reckless behavior.
